content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper uses reinforcement learning to learn the optimal strategy of a leader in a Stackelberg. 
In a Stackelberg game, there is one leader and multiple followers, the leader commits a strategy and the followers then choose their actions basing on the leader's committed strategy.
By assuming the followers use variant of no-regret learning dynamic, the paper formulates the problem as a partially observable markov decision process (POMDP) and apply the actor-critic method to learn a Bayesian coarse correlated equilibrium. 
Experiment results are provided for normal form (Stackelberg) game, matrix design game, sequential pricing and simple allocation mechanism.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength. The use of reinforcement learning to learn solution concept in games/auctions is a hot topic and the paper continues this line of work. The experiments of the paper indicates the proposed method can reach good solutions under toy examples.


Weakness. T

(1) The proposed method is only verified on toy examples. That is, the experiments set up seems to be too simple and it is unclear whether the method scale up.

(2) There is no theoretical guarantee.

(3) There are too many assumptions made in the paper and many of them are not well-supported. In particular

> (3.1) The assumption of no-regret followers seems unreasonable (despite I am aware some recent work in the literature).  
> (3.2) The solution concept of Bayesian coarse correlated equilibrium might be too weak for applications. Especially in a stackelberg game, the stackelberg equilibrium makes much more sense than the correlated equilibrium.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8NGf
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments and wish to answer some of the concerns raised.

(1) The proposed method is only verified on toy examples. That is, the experiments set up seems to be too simple and it is unclear whether the method scale up.

In the setting of “Sequential price mechanisms with messages” the strategy space of the leader is very complex as it needs to learn a communication protocol between players and the mechanism as well as the rules of a multi-step pricing scheme. To the best of our knowledge, having the strategy space be the space of all such mechanisms goes far beyond the strategy spaces in prior work. In addition, a subsequent paper (Brero et al. 2022) makes use of our framework to design platforms that mitigate collusion. In that scenario, the strategy space of the leader consists of policies mapping 25 possible observations to 5 actions (5^{25} possible mappings).

(2) There is no theoretical guarantee.

Our guarantee is of the form - given an RL algorithm that can solve the POMDP problem, solving our formulated Stackelberg POMDP will result in an optimal leader’s strategy.

(3.1) The assumption of no-regret followers seems unreasonable (despite I am aware some recent work in the literature).

We model the followers as agents using no-regret dynamics to update their strategies due to the strong convergence guarantees they provide. This is not necessary for the framework, however,  and we can use other methods to learn follower strategies.  In fact, a subsequent paper (Brero et al. 2022) uses Q-learning to update the followers’ strategies and shows that, experimentally, this works as well. In general, our Stackelberg POMDP is well formed as long as the re-equilibration behavior of the followers can be modeled through Markovian dynamics and integrated into the Stackelberg POMDP states. We have added a comment on this in our revision (Observation 4.1).

(3.2) The solution concept of Bayesian coarse correlated equilibrium might be too weak for applications. Especially in a stackelberg game, the stackelberg equilibrium makes much more sense than the correlated equilibrium.

Just to be sure: we learn a Stackelberg equilibrium, where we adopt BCCE as the behavior model of the followers (we need some follower equilibrium concept with multiple followers). In this sense, we learn a Stackelberg-BCCE. In regard to BCCE: since we deal with Bayesian settings where agents have private types, a Bayesian solution concept is appropriate. When our methods are applied to non-Bayesian settings, then the solution concept would change to the non-Bayesian counterpart. We note that if the agents use “no swap regret” to update their strategy instead of “no external regret,” then the solution concepts would further change from coarse correlated equilibrium to correlated equilibrium. We chose to model agents as no external regret because no external regret algorithms have stronger convergence guarantees than their no swap regret counterparts.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a generic approach for learning Stackelberg games by formulating them as single-agent POMDPs. Some optimality characterizations are established in theory. Experimentally, the proposed formulation is combined with MAPPO to show fast convergence on a bunch of Stackelberg games.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

* Learning Stackelberg equilibria is a hard challenge for multi-agent RL / games. (Personally, I feel even reliably evaluating progress for this problem is challenging on large-scale instances.) The paper develops a new general formulation as single-agent POMDPs, which can be combined with deep RL algorithms to give algorithms for learning Stackelberg equilibria. 

Weaknesses:

Overall, I’m quite confused and concerned about what the proposed formulation really is and how/why it is better than existing approaches, in terms of both the formulation, theory, and the experiments.

* On the formulation/theory side, I think Section 3 & 4 is substantially lacking in clarity and rigor. From these descriptions, I didn’t really understand what the reformulated POMDP is, given a Stackelberg game of interest. Examples of questions I have:
  - What does the time step $\tau$ in the POMDP represent? Is it used to model the learning progress of leaders / followers using some learning algorithm within the original Stackelberg game (SG), or the same as the time step in the original SG?
  - What is partially observable? In my understanding a standard POMDP consists of a hidden state $s$ and observation $o$ emitted from the latent state; however Section 3 did not specify what $o$ is, but an $o$ is involved in Eq(2).
  - Section 3 and Section 4 seem to be proposing two different POMDPs, one with exactly optimal (equilibrium-playing) follower, one with follower learning the equilibrium using no-regret algorithms. What is the relationship?
  - The theoretical results are lacking in mathematical rigor (for example, what does “As T goes large” mean). Some proofs involve “$\approx$” that are not defined, but are the key parts of the proofs in my opinion. For example, the first “$\approx$” on Page 13 relates empirical counts to approximate true probability. This typically requires stating clearly what the error measure is, and also typically requires assumptions such as reachability, none addressed in the proof.
  - Observation 3.1 / Proposition 4.1 are not “proof of convergence” as claimed in Section 1, as they does not involve any concrete algorithm on the leader’s side, which is the main challenge for learning Stackelberg equilibria.

* For experiments, there appear to be no comparisons at all with existing methods (i.e. other methods that do not leverage the proposed POMDP reformulation). The only comparison is MAPPO vs. PPO (later uses a centralized critic network), both under the proposed POMDP formulation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall I feel the paper is substantially lacking in clarity for the description of the core formulation; For concrete comments please find in the above “Strengths and Weaknesses” section.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes to learn Stackelberg games by formulating them as single-agent POMDPs. While seemingly an interesting idea, none of the formulation/theory/experiments are convincing or even stated clearly enough to give a sense of what the proposed formulation is, or why it is better than existing work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4485 by Reviewer ChVd

content.title: Response to Reviewer ChVd
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments and want to answer some of the concerns.

We are aware our formulation is written very generally since it is supposed to capture many different settings. We think some of the confusion might be alleviated by going over Appendix C, which gives a detailed POMDP formulation to our “Sequential Price Mechanisms with Messages” setting (the most complicated one we consider).

“What does the time step in the POMDP represent? Is it used to model the learning progress of leaders/followers using some learning algorithm within the original Stackelberg game (SG), or the same as the time step in the original SG?” 

It is used for both. First, in the “Equilibrium sub-episodes,” we run the SG in order for the followers to learn the equilibrium, and then we run the SG during the “Reward sub-episodes” in order for the leader to collect their reward. The leader’s optimization problem is modeled by this POMDP. 

“What is partially observable?”

The followers’ strategies are always an unobserved part of the state. In addition to this, in Bayesian games where followers’ types are drawn from a distribution, their type is also unobservable to the leader. Please see Appendix C for a concrete example.

“Section 3 and Section 4 seem to be proposing two different POMDPs, one with exactly optimal (equilibrium-playing) follower, one with follower learning the equilibrium using no-regret algorithms. What is the relationship?”

In Section 3, the formulation is not of a POMDP but of a Markov game. We show how to formulate this problem as a single-agent optimization problem, which *is not* a POMDP. In Section 4, we show how we can formulate the problem as a POMDP by computing the followers’ strategies by repeatedly simulating the Stackelberg game.

“The theoretical results are lacking in mathematical rigor (for example, what does “As T goes large” mean). Some proofs involve “≈” that are not defined, but are the key parts of the proofs in my opinion.”

By “as T goes large,” we mean the standard no-regret convergence/equilibrium convergence guarantees of the literature (as the regret goes to 0 as T goes to infinity, we have that the strategies converge to an equilibrium as T goes to infinity, etc.). We added rigor and precision to the revised paper by defining Approximate BCCE (definition 3), Approximate optimal leader strategy (definition 4), and asymptotic convergence to optimal leader strategy (definition 5). 

The reason we can use ≈ in the proof of Proposition 2.1 is given in Footnote 10 in the previously submitted version. By the Glivenko–Cantelli Theorem, the estimation error goes to 0 as T goes to infinity. Since the estimation error is multiplied by a bounded term, we can disregard the term. In the revised manuscript, we used an explicit term for the misestimation error and moved the explanation this term is o(1) from the footnote.

“Observation 3.1 / Proposition 4.1 are not “proof of convergence” as claimed in Section 1, as they do not involve any concrete algorithm on the leader’s side, which is the main challenge for learning Stackelberg equilibria.”

Given that this is Deep RL there are no absolute guarantees. However, our theorem shows that IF an algorithm converges for the leader, then it converges to a Stackelberg equilibrium. This becomes no different from a standard RL problem and standard assumptions in regard to exploration suffice.

“For experiments, there appear to be no comparisons at all with existing methods (i.e. other methods that do not leverage the proposed POMDP reformulation). The only comparison is MAPPO vs. PPO (later uses a centralized critic network), both under the proposed POMDP formulation.”

We are not aware of existing methods applicable to settings like the mSPM one, where the strategy space of the leader is very complex as it needs to learn an emergent communication protocol between agents and learn to perform a multi-step pricing scheme. At the same time, existing approaches would directly find optimal solutions in our normal-form games as they are tailored to these settings.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The idea of the paper is to use learning methods to compute equilibria in certain types of Stackelberg games (games with a leader-follower structure). Usually in Stackelberg games with multiple followers, the assumption is that once the leader strategy is fixed, the followers will play a Nash equilibrium. A major distinction in this paper is that they play a Bayesian coarse-correlated equilibrium instead -- this solution concept is one that can be reached by joint online learning even in general-sum games. They then reduce the Stackelberg problem to a POMDP for just the leader, which has a "two-timescale" flavor. Solving this POMDP gives the leader's Stackelberg policy. The authors give experimental evidence for their approach in some simple settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses: the choice of games to study definitely has the feeling of "toy" examples, and there are no extremely shocking or mind-expanding theoretical results. This is fine given what the paper is trying to achieve, but it is a weakness. The approach also requires that the  follower's game be such that an actual no-regret algorithm can be applied, which rules out e.g. games where the follower policies are neural networks.

Strengths: the paper brings some much needed clarity to a topic which is important but relatively neglected in the literature. The framework seems genuinely useful and a better starting point than much existing work for Stackelberg games or even games with a more nebulous leader-follower structure.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work is quite clearly written and is original and novel in what it accomplishes, even if the results are not hype-worthy or incredibly exciting. The quality is fairly high.

Reproducibility: The experiment section seems good. This is only a minor complaint, but some mention in the paper of the use of random seeds seems warranted, as this is always an issue with RL.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Designing policies or mechanisms in multi-agent settings where some agents can respond to the policies is increasingly relevant. An increasing number of recent works try to use reinforcement learning in games which somehow have a leader-follower structure. For example, Zheng et al. "The Ai Economist", "AI-driven Prices for Sustainable Production Markets" by Danassis et al., as well as some of the mechanism design works or related work cited by this paper.

Mostly these take an ad-hoc approach of applying off-the-shelf MARL (which may converge to Nash or may have no convergence guarantees at all). So this paper's reduction to the POMDP seems like it could be a useful contribution for many of these types of problems. I think the community would benefit from having this work published.

We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments and wish to answer some of the concerns.

“The approach also requires that the follower's game be such that an actual no-regret algorithm can be applied, which rules out e.g. games where the follower policies are neural networks.”

We model the followers as agents using no-regret dynamics to update their strategies due to the strong convergence guarantees they provide. The computational framework is more general, however, and we can use other methods to update followers’ strategies. In fact, a subsequent paper (Brero et al. 2022) uses Q-learning to update the followers’ strategies and shows that, experimentally, this works as well. Indeed, our Stackelberg POMDP is well formed as long as the re-equilibration behavior of the followers can be modeled through Markovian dynamics and integrated into the Stackelberg POMDP states. We have added a comment on this in our revision (Observation 4.1).

“the choice of games to study definitely has the feeling of "toy" examples”

Our goal in this paper was to test increasingly complex settings ranging from normal form games with one follower to sequential allocation problems with multiple followers. We also note that a follow-up work (Brero et al. 2022) uses our framework to design platforms that mitigate collusion. In that scenario, the strategy space of the leader consists of policies mapping 25 possible observations to 5 actions (5^{25} possible mappings).

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors present a reinforcement-learning method for finding equilibria in Stackelberg stochastic games. In this setting, one agent, commonly referred to as a leader, selects parameters of a game, in which other agents, called followers, attain an equilibrium. This (sub-)solution-concept the authors consider is the Bayesian coarse correlated equilibrium. After giving a formal definition, the authors introduce two variants of the PPO algorithm to approximate the optimal leader strategy, while the followers use no-regret-dynamics to find the equilibrium. The resulting algorithm is further tested on four classes of Stackelberg games of increasing complexity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper builds on existing literature and is well motivated. The presentation is elegant and easy to follow, with maybe just one minor thing: I found some portions perhaps overly repetitive. For example, the first paragraph of section 5.4 just repeats the definition given in section 2.1. Besides that, all concepts are nicely explained. The theoretical results are intuitive and as far as I can tell, they seem correct to me. 

I enjoyed the theoretical part of the paper, though I feel the experimental results might be further improved. The authors consider several standard settings, for which (if I am not wrong) already exist algorithms solving them. Yet, the experiments lack any comparison to these baselines. Besides, I wonder how well the authors’ approach scales with size of these scenarios in terms of strategy spaces or number of players. Are there some games where the known methods fail due to their limited scalability, or are unusable for other reasons, where the presented algorithm can provide reasonable strategies? I’m curious about this also because the domains the experiments are solving appear rather small. 

Also, I understand that the optimal policy in the Stackelberg POMDP achieves the same utility as in the original game, yet it seems the text does not discuss if there are any guarantees of reaching this optimal policy. Do the PPO-based algorithms the authors consider promise any convergence? 

I believe it may also help the reader to familiarize themselves with this work if the authors emphasized more (eg in the introduction) that the equilibrium they aim to find is the Bayesian-CCE Stackelberg equilibrium rather than the (perhaps more common) strong Stackelberg-Nash equilibrium.

Typo: Prop 4.1: “Equation equation 1.”
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity - The paper is structured well and is easy to understand most of the time. However, several important details about the experiments were omitted from the main text and instead deferred to the captions of the figures or tables, making the overall presentation slightly less clear.

Quality - The results look correct and interesting, but, reiterating my previous thought, the work lacks any comparison with standard benchmarks for solving the scenarios the authors consider. For example, in Section 5.4 the authors mention optimal mechanism to solve the game, and mention that the learning algorithm was able to imitate it in 6 of 10 runs. What happened during the other runs?

Novelty - The reformulation of the problem as the Stackelberg POMDP seems sufficiently novel to me. 

Reproducibility - The results are probably  hard to reproduce based solely on the paper, since no specific values of the parameters used in the experiments are mentioned in the text. However, the authors promise to make the code available after the paper is published.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents results in an organized and easy to understand way. Obviously, the main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a new game-theoretic algorithm combining single-agent reinforcement learning with Stackelberg games. However, the experimental section does not provide any comparison to existing methods, without which the computational merits of this algorithm are difficult to assess.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Qovy
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments and wish to answer some of their concerns.

“The authors consider several standard settings, for which (if I am not wrong) already exist algorithms solving them. Yet, the experiments lack any comparison to these baselines.”

As far as we know, the only scenario that was considered in previous works that uses Stackelberg computation is that of choosing strategies in matrix form games, and the other scenarios are novel. In particular, we do not know of any scenarios that consider learning a communication protocol such as the “simple allocation mechanisms” and “sequential price mechanisms with messages,” where in the latter the strategy space of the leader is very complex as it needs to learn an emergent communication protocol between agents and learn to perform a multi-step pricing scheme. To the best of our knowledge, having the strategy space be the space of all such mechanisms goes far beyond the strategy spaces that other papers have dealt with. Standard approaches cannot be applied in these complex settings while they trivially find optimal solutions for our normal-form games. 

“Besides, I wonder how well the authors’ approach scales with size of these scenarios in terms of strategy spaces or number of players.”

As noted above, the strategy space of the leader is quite complicated in some of the experiments. In the messageSPM setting we consider, the strategy space consists of mapping message profiles to sequential price mechanisms, which determine the order in which agents are visited and the price (continuous!) to quote. In addition, a follow-up work (Brero et al. 2022) uses our framework to design platforms that mitigate collusion. In that scenario, the strategy space of the leader consists of policies mapping 25 possible observations to 5 actions (5^{25} possible mappings).

“the authors mention optimal mechanism to solve the game, and mention that the learning algorithm was able to imitate it in 6 of 10 runs. What happened during the other runs?”

We encountered numerical instabilities in those runs, which we now know was due to an erroneously high learning rate. We have fixed this issue by reducing the learning rate by a factor of 100 and now learn optimal SPMs 100% of the time. This is updated in the revised paper.

content.title: Paper Revision
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments, which inspired our paper revision. Most importantly:

1. We added rigor and precision to the revised paper by defining approximate BCCE (definition 3), approximate optimal leader strategy (definition 4), and asymptotic convergence to optimal leader strategy (definition 5). 

2. We added a comment on the generality of our Stackelberg POMDP with respect to the followers' re-equilibration behavior (observation 4.1).  

3. We updated the mSPM simulation results. In our previous version, we learned optimal mSPMs only in 6 out of 10 runs. This was due to numerical instabilities, which we now know was due to an erroneously high learning rate. We have fixed this issue by reducing the learning rate by a factor of 100 and now learn optimal SPMs 100% of the time.
